title: What Are Postbiotics? A Parent’s Guide
summary: Learn what postbiotics mean, how they differ from probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics, and what parents can check when reading product labels.
body_markdown:
If you have seen the term while comparing microbiome products, you may be asking, what are postbiotics? In the scientific consensus definition, a postbiotic is a preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit on the host. That definition is more precise than simply calling something fermented or connected with microbes. The name alone does not identify a specific ingredient or establish what a product does.


[Ask a question about product terminology](https://persephone.bio/pages/contact)


## What does postbiotic mean in science?


The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) published the consensus definition in 2021. Its wording has three useful parts: a preparation; inanimate microorganisms and/or their components; and a health benefit. A reader needs all three elements to understand how the term is being used. A product that contains microbial material does not automatically meet this definition, and the category does not by itself tell you whether a product is appropriate for a particular person.


“Preparation” points to a defined material rather than a vague reference to a production process. “Inanimate microorganisms and/or their components” distinguishes the concept from products centered on live microbes. The final part, a health benefit, matters too: microbial material or a history of fermentation alone does not establish such a benefit. The evidence has to relate to the specific preparation and context being discussed.


The[ISAPP consensus statement in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41575-021-00440-6) explains the definition and its boundaries. It is a helpful reference when a label, article, or conversation uses “postbiotic” broadly. Instead of treating the term as a guarantee, you can compare the description with the scientific definition and then look for ingredient-level information.


For example, a page might say “fermented ingredient” but not explain what the finished preparation contains. Another might name a defined preparation and point to research about a particular benefit. The second description answers more questions, but readers still need to check whether the research actually concerns the same material and use. A label term is a starting point for inquiry, not the whole evidence story.


## How do probiotics, prebiotics, postbiotics, and synbiotics differ?


These terms describe related but distinct concepts. The table is a plain-language orientation, not a way to classify an unnamed product from one phrase. A formal definition and the evidence for an individual product may include details beyond the short descriptions below.


Term Core idea Questions to check


Probiotic Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host. Which microorganism or strain? What amount, intended use, and evidence?


Prebiotic A substrate selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit. What is the substrate, and what evidence applies to the stated context?


Postbiotic A preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit. What is the preparation, and does evidence address that material and benefit?


Synbiotic A mixture of live microorganisms and selectively utilized substrate or substrates that confers a health benefit. Which components are combined, and what evidence concerns the combination?


ISAPP has published consensus definitions for[probiotics](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrgastro.2016.110) ,[prebiotics](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrgastro.2017.75) , and[synbiotics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41575-020-0344-2) , as well as postbiotics. These definitions help distinguish a live microorganism, a selectively utilized substrate, inanimate microbial material, and a combination involving live microbes plus substrate. A shared connection to the microbiome does not make the terms interchangeable.


A practical first question is: what is the preparation centered on? If it is live microorganisms, the probiotic concept may be relevant. If it is a substrate selectively used by host microorganisms, prebiotic may apply. If it is inanimate microbial material or components, postbiotic may be the intended term. A combination of live microbes and substrates may be described as a synbiotic. This is only an orientation; ingredient details and evidence still matter.


## Does fermented mean postbiotic?


No. Fermentation describes a process in which microorganisms transform substances. A fermented food or ingredient may involve live microbes, microbial components, and substances created during fermentation. Knowing that fermentation occurred does not tell you, by itself, what is in the finished preparation or whether it fits the postbiotic definition.


Consider two hypothetical descriptions. One says only “fermented ingredient.” The other identifies a defined preparation of inanimate microorganisms or their components and describes evidence for a health benefit. The second gives information relevant to the definition, though the evidence still needs to match the claim. The process word alone cannot fill in missing details about the final material.


This distinction also helps when reading about food. “Fermented” can accurately describe how a food was made without meaning the food is a postbiotic. Separate three questions: Was fermentation used? What is in the final preparation? What evidence supports the stated benefit? An answer to the first question does not automatically answer the next two.


## What can the word postbiotic tell you—and what can it not?


Used in the strict consensus sense, the term points to a defined preparation involving inanimate microorganisms and/or their components and a health benefit. That is useful category information. It is not a complete description of an ingredient, finished product, or intended use.


On its own, the word does not identify the organism, components, preparation method, amount per serving, storage directions, or population studied. It also does not prove that findings about one preparation apply to another. Nor does it mean that every person will have the same experience or that the product fits every use.


When you encounter the term, look for a more specific ingredient description and the context for any claim. If research is cited, check whether the study examined the same preparation, population, and use. A result about a related organism or a different formulation may provide background, but it does not automatically answer questions about the product in front of you.


It can help to separate three levels of information: what an ingredient is, what research has examined, and what a finished product claims. These levels may overlap, but they are not identical. A study can offer useful context without answering every question about a product. Transparent communication makes those boundaries visible rather than relying on a scientific-sounding category name.


## How can parents assess a postbiotic claim?


Start with what can be checked on the label or product page, rather than the strength of a headline. These questions make a broad claim more concrete:


- **What exactly is the preparation?** Look for a named ingredient and a description of the material or components. If the information is broad, note that rather than guessing what is present.
- **Is the nature of the preparation clear?** Postbiotic is not simply another name for a live probiotic. Look for an explanation that makes the distinction understandable.
- **What benefit is being discussed?** Identify the specific claim and its context. The category name alone does not establish every possible benefit.
- **Does the evidence match the preparation?** Compare the research material with the named ingredient. Evidence about a different strain, process, or formulation may not answer the same question.
- **Who and what were studied?** Note the population, amount, duration, and intended use. Avoid assuming that a result in one setting applies to a different age group or situation.
- **Are directions and use details clear?** Read serving instructions, amount, storage information, and age guidance. Similar terminology does not make two products interchangeable.
- **Can you find quality and safety information?** If key details are missing, ask the manufacturer or a qualified health professional for clarification.


Make the review practical by writing down the label’s exact wording. Separate what is stated from what is not: for example, “ingredient named; preparation form not stated.” This is more useful than assuming that the material is live or inanimate. It also gives you a focused question to take to a manufacturer or healthcare professional.


Next, follow the evidence trail in order. Start with the ingredient description, then read any study or scientific statement cited by the manufacturer. Ask whether it examines the same preparation, population, and use. Similar terminology does not make two materials identical, and a citation is a starting point for assessment rather than automatic endorsement.


For an infant or toddler supplement, discuss questions about ingredients, age suitability, or use with your pediatrician. A product page cannot provide individualized medical guidance. Persephone’s[safety information](https://persephone.bio/pages/safety) and[FAQ](https://persephone.bio/pages/faq) offer places to review product-specific information and common questions.


## How should you compare two labels that use similar terms?


Imagine comparing two products with “microbiome support” language. Product A names a microbial ingredient but does not explain whether the material is live or inanimate. Product B describes a preparation, gives an amount per serving, and refers to research. Product B provides more information to evaluate; that does not automatically make its claims established or prove that it is the right choice.


For a fair comparison, make a side-by-side note rather than relying on memory. Record the ingredient name, preparation form, amount, intended population, directions, and evidence cited. Mark missing information as “not stated.” This simple step separates what a label says from what you might infer from scientific-sounding language.


Then check whether the evidence concerns the specific material in the product. A study about a live strain cannot automatically establish a claim for an inanimate preparation. Likewise, evidence for one postbiotic preparation cannot automatically be transferred to a different one. The relevant comparison is not just category versus category; it is the actual ingredient and use being discussed.


### A worked label-review example


Suppose one label says “postbiotic blend” without another description. A second names a preparation, describes it as inanimate microbial material, states the amount per serving, and links to a study. You do not need to decide which is better to note that the first leaves identity, amount, and evidence unclear while the second supplies more points to verify.


For the second label, read the cited research. Does it study that same preparation? Is the population similar? Does the product use the same amount and directions? If you cannot tell, record the gap and ask the manufacturer or a qualified health professional. A reference is useful, but it does not automatically substantiate every claim made about a finished product.


If the study concerns a related but different preparation, it may still offer background. Describe that relationship accurately: it is evidence about a related material, not proof that the finished product has the same effect. Keeping those statements separate is a useful habit when evaluating any science-based label.


## How is a postbiotic different from a synbiotic?


A postbiotic and a synbiotic describe different kinds of preparations. Under the consensus definitions, a postbiotic involves inanimate microorganisms and/or their components. A synbiotic combines live microorganisms with selectively utilized substrate or substrates. The classification depends on the preparation, not simply on its connection to gut health.


Persephone describes its infant and toddler products as synbiotics: they combine a probiotic and a prebiotic. This article does not describe those products as postbiotics or suggest that postbiotics are an ingredient in them. For the company’s explanation of its approach, see[Persephone’s science information](https://persephone.bio/pages/our-science) . You can also read the guide to[HMOs in a synbiotic formulation](https://persephone.bio/blogs/news/what-are-hmos-and-why-they-matter-in-our-synbiotic) .


In this context, “synergistic synbiotic” refers to a scientific concept involving precision-matched probiotics and prebiotics; it is not another name for postbiotic. The terms describe different composition concepts. Keeping them separate helps readers understand what a label says without assuming every microbiome-related ingredient is the same.


A company can discuss postbiotics as a scientific topic while describing a particular product as a synbiotic. An educational article about one category does not establish that category as an ingredient in a product. Check current product information for composition rather than inferring it from nearby content or shared terminology.


## What should parents do when information is unclear?


First, identify the exact point that is unclear. Is it the ingredient name, whether the material is live or inanimate, the amount in a serving, or the evidence for a stated benefit? A specific question is easier to answer than a general request to explain the label.


Second, keep the label or product page available and check its full directions and supporting material. If an answer relies on a study, ask whether it examined the same preparation and population. If it does not, treat that as a limit on what the evidence can tell you, rather than assuming the results transfer.


Third, for decisions involving an infant or toddler, consider discussing the product with your child’s pediatrician. This can be helpful when you have questions about age, ingredients, or how a supplement fits your family’s circumstances. The aim is clear, relevant information—not making every new term a source of worry.


Persephone describes its infant and toddler formulations as synbiotics, combining a probiotic and a prebiotic. To review current information, visit the[science overview](https://persephone.bio/pages/our-science) and[FAQ](https://persephone.bio/pages/faq) , or[contact the team](https://persephone.bio/pages/contact) with a specific question. Product descriptions and formulations should be checked directly rather than inferred from a general microbiome term.


## Frequently asked questions


### Are postbiotics alive?


The consensus definition describes inanimate microorganisms and/or their components in a preparation. That distinguishes postbiotics from probiotics, which are live microorganisms meeting their accepted definition.


### Are postbiotics the same as probiotics?


No. The terms describe different categories. A probiotic is live; a postbiotic is a defined preparation involving inanimate microorganisms or their components, with a health benefit in context.


### Does every fermented food count as a postbiotic?


No. Fermentation is a process, and that process alone does not establish that the finished food or ingredient meets the postbiotic definition. The preparation and evidence matter.


### Does the term tell me whether a product is appropriate for my child?


No. The word alone does not establish age suitability or whether a product fits an individual child’s needs. Check current directions and ask your pediatrician when you need guidance.


### Are postbiotics included in Persephone’s infant and toddler products?


Persephone describes its products as synbiotics that combine a probiotic and a prebiotic. This article does not identify postbiotics as an ingredient. Review current product information for formulation details.


[Explore Persephone’s science information](https://persephone.bio/pages/our-science)


## What should parents remember about postbiotics?


Postbiotic has a specific scientific definition, but the word alone cannot tell you everything about a preparation, its evidence, or its relevance to a product. Look for transparent ingredient and use information, compare research with the specific preparation, and ask a healthcare professional when you need guidance for your child.
